title: Henry IV, Part 2
author: William Shakespeare
openingChapterLabel: Act 1, Scene 1 — Warkworth, before Northumberland's castle
openingText: [After the battle of Shrewsbury.] Rumour, painted full of tongues, opens the play with confused reports of the rebels' fortunes and Hotspur's death.
about:
Henry IV, Part 2 picks up the day after the battle of Shrewsbury, where Prince Hal killed the rebel Hotspur in single combat at the end of Part 1. The Earl of Northumberland, Hotspur's father, learns of his son's death and begins to gather a new revolt with the Archbishop of York. The king, increasingly ill and sleepless, watches the rebellion grow. Prince Hal stays at the tavern with Falstaff, half-out of mourning for his old life, half-aware that the crown is coming to him soon.

The play follows two stories in alternation. In the political plot, Prince John of Lancaster meets the rebels at Gaultree Forest, agrees to terms, and then arrests them on a technicality and executes them. In the comic plot, Falstaff travels through Gloucestershire recruiting old men into the king's army, fleecing Justice Shallow, and continuing his old career of borrowing and lying. The two plots converge when the king dies in the Jerusalem Chamber, Hal succeeds him as Henry V, and the new king meets Falstaff at his coronation procession with the line that ends a friendship: 'I know thee not, old man.'

Shakespeare wrote Part 2 in late 1597 or early 1598, as the immediate sequel to the enormously popular Part 1. It is darker, slower, and quieter than its predecessor — full of sickness, old men remembering their youth, and the long approach of a death. It contains some of Shakespeare's finest verse on aging and decline, and the moment a Prince of Wales becomes a king.

angleCards.title: Hal and Falstaff.
angleCards.text: Part 2 is the long approach to the moment Hal becomes king and rejects Falstaff in public. Every Falstaff scene is the comedy of a friendship the audience already knows is going to end.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the Hal–Falstaff relationship through Part 2 as the long preparation for the rejection — and decide what Shakespeare wants us to feel when the moment arrives.

angleCards.title: An aging country.
angleCards.text: Henry IV, Part 2 is full of old men: a dying king, a senile justice, an aging soldier, a fat knight who keeps lying about his age. The play is about a country running out of breath at the same time as its leader.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Part 2 as Shakespeare's play about aging — the king's sickness, Shallow's reminiscences, Falstaff's denial — and see how the political plot rhymes with the personal one.

angleCards.title: The rebellion that ends in a trick.
angleCards.text: Prince John meets the rebels at Gaultree Forest, accepts their terms, and arrests them when they disperse. It is one of the morally ugliest moments in any Shakespeare history. Watch what the play does with it.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Gaultree Forest scene with attention to what Shakespeare lets stand without comment — the broken pledge, the executions — and what it tells us about the Lancastrian regime Hal is about to inherit.

angleCards.title: The coronation.
angleCards.text: The last five minutes of the play are Hal in his coronation robes meeting Falstaff in the street. 'I know thee not, old man' is one of the most famous, most argued-about lines in Shakespeare. Some readers think it is the moment Hal becomes king. Others think it is the moment Hal stops being human.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the final coronation scene closely — Hal's rejection of Falstaff — and decide whether Shakespeare presents it as necessary, as cruel, or as both.

cast.name: King Henry IV
cast.description: Once the usurper Bolingbroke, now sick and sleepless, haunted by Richard II's death and the long civil wars his crown has produced. He spends most of the play offstage, ill, and dies in the Jerusalem Chamber in Act 4. The crown changes hands during the scene where his son thinks he is already dead.

cast.name: Prince Hal
cast.description: The future Henry V. He continues the apparent dissipation of Part 1 in the early acts, half out of grief at his father's illness, then is reconciled to him at the deathbed, and rejects Falstaff in the closing scene as he assumes the crown. The play is the bridge between the wild prince and the warrior king.

cast.name: Sir John Falstaff
cast.description: The old, vast, lying, brilliant knight from Part 1, now a captain with his own commission. He travels to Gloucestershire to recruit, fleeces Justice Shallow of a thousand pounds, and waits in the street for the new king to come and ennoble him. He receives instead the rejection that ends the play and, in spirit, the friendship that ran through both parts.

cast.name: Prince John of Lancaster
cast.description: Hal's younger brother, sent to negotiate with the rebels at Gaultree Forest. He gives his word, takes their surrender, and then has them arrested and executed. He is the cold, capable Lancastrian Shakespeare contrasts with his charming brother.

cast.name: The Lord Chief Justice
cast.description: The chief judge of the kingdom, who has once sent Hal to prison for striking him in court. Hal, on becoming king, walks into the council expecting trouble and instead embraces him, confirming the Lord Chief Justice as his closest political advisor. The scene is the public turn from Falstaff to law.

cast.name: Justice Shallow
cast.description: An elderly justice of the peace in Gloucestershire, vainglorious and full of unreliable memories of his student days carousing with Falstaff. He lends Falstaff a thousand pounds in the hope of preferment under the new king. He is one of Shakespeare's most affectionate sketches of provincial aging.

acclaim.quote: Shakespeare has put as much character and passion into Justice Shallow as into any of his serious characters.
The rejection of Falstaff is the necessary and proper conclusion of the play, but it cannot be played without pain.
acclaim.context: Oxford Lectures on Poetry, 'The Rejection of Falstaff,' 1909

whyItMatters.title: The Play of Old Men
whyItMatters.body: Henry IV, Part 2 is one of Shakespeare's quietest plays and one of his most insistent on age. The king is sick from the opening; he cannot sleep; he is dying through three acts before he finally dies in the fourth. Falstaff has been old in Part 1 — he calls himself old constantly — but in Part 2 the joke begins to wear out. He limps. He needs a page. The doctor sends him bad reports of his urine. He goes to Gloucestershire and sits with Justice Shallow under the trees while two old men remember their youth in fragments neither of them quite has straight. The recruiting scene is built around feeble, mouldy, bullcalf, and shadow — Falstaff's catalogue of half-dead men he conscripts into the king's army. Even the rebellion is an old man's affair: Northumberland mourning a dead son, the Archbishop of York fighting old battles. Shakespeare wrote the play in his early thirties. It is the work of a young man who has been listening very closely to the old.

whyItMatters.title: The Rejection of Falstaff
whyItMatters.body: The most famous moment in Part 2 is its last. The new king Henry V walks in procession to his coronation. Falstaff has galloped up from Gloucestershire to meet him, sure that his hour has come. He waves. He calls out. Hal stops, looks at him, and delivers some of the coldest lines in Shakespeare: 'I know thee not, old man. Fall to thy prayers. / How ill white hairs become a fool and jester!' He banishes Falstaff from his presence on pain of death and walks on. The scene has been argued about for four centuries. A. C. Bradley wrote a whole essay on it called 'The Rejection of Falstaff,' arguing that it is necessary in the play and unbearable on the stage. Orson Welles made a whole film, Chimes at Midnight, that ends on the rejection. Productions for centuries have tried to soften the line; nothing softens it. Shakespeare wrote a comedy whose closing scene is one of the most painful moments in any of his plays, performed by a king the play has spent five acts asking us to believe in.

whyItMatters.title: The Lancastrian Cost
whyItMatters.body: Part 2 includes the moment Shakespeare's audiences understood as the formal birth of the Lancastrian regime that runs through Henry V, Henry VI, and Richard III. The way it happens is unsavoury. At Gaultree Forest, Prince John of Lancaster — Hal's cold younger brother — receives the rebels' grievances, agrees to address them all, and proposes a toast of peace. The rebels disband their army. The moment they do, Prince John arrests their leaders and sends them to execution. Shakespeare lets the scene end with Prince John saying, blandly, that he never promised not to punish them for treason — only to address their grievances. No one in the play criticises him. The Archbishop of York, the rebel Hastings, and the rest are led off. Shakespeare gives the moment no big speeches and no on-stage horror; he lets it stand as the price the Lancastrian crown is willing to pay for its peace. Hal is going to inherit a state that does this kind of thing, and the play wants the audience to notice.
